subject: Archaeology
title: Radiocarbon Dating Explained
description: A micro-lesson that makes Radiocarbon Dating Explained usable.

hook.text: Every living thing absorbs a radioactive form of carbon. When it dies, that carbon starts ticking like a clock.

buildup.text: Carbon-14 decays at a known rate — half of it disappears every 5,730 years. Measuring what is left reveals the age.

discovery.text: Willard Libby invented the technique in 1949 and won the Nobel Prize. It revolutionized archaeology overnight.

twist.text: It only works on organic material — bone, wood, charcoal, and shells. Stones and metals cannot be radiocarbon dated.

climax.text: Modern accelerator mass spectrometry can date a single grain of wheat and needs samples thousands of times smaller.

punchline.text: A ticking atomic clock hides inside every bone and seed.

quiz.question: What is the half-life of Carbon-14?
